variants.title: Follow a document into the index
variants.context: A Lucene document is a set of named fields. Define what each field must answer, analyze or encode the value, write the access paths (postings, points, doc values, stored fields), then open or refresh a reader to publish a point-in-time view.
variants.prompt: A product record is added to a Lucene index. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Define the field contract: relevance, exact filter, phrase, range, sort, or retrieval.
Analyze human text into tokens and encode exact values and numbers.
Write postings, points, doc values, and stored fields into immutable segments.
Open or refresh a reader and search the new point-in-time view.

variants.hint: Nothing can be queried that was not decided at index time.
variants.explanation: Contract → analyze → write access paths → publish a reader. A query can only use structures created at index time.

variants.title: Follow a document into the index
variants.context: A Lucene document is a set of named fields. Define what each field must answer, analyze or encode the value, write the access paths (postings, points, doc values, stored fields), then open or refresh a reader to publish a point-in-time view.
variants.prompt: The team wants phrase search on descriptions. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Record that descriptions need full-text relevance with positions.
Run the description through the analyzer tied to that field.
Index postings with positions so phrases can match.
Refresh a reader so searches see the new documents.

variants.hint: Positions must be written before a phrase query can ever use them.
variants.explanation: A phrase needs indexed positions, not the stored string. TextField’s standard type indexes them.

variants.title: Follow a document into the index
variants.context: A Lucene document is a set of named fields. Define what each field must answer, analyze or encode the value, write the access paths (postings, points, doc values, stored fields), then open or refresh a reader to publish a point-in-time view.
variants.prompt: Country codes must filter exactly and sort. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Decide the value needs exact matching and ordering, not tokenization.
Keep the code as one exact term rather than analyzing it.
Write a StringField plus a sorted doc-values field.

variants.hint: An identifier is not human language; it should not be tokenized.
variants.explanation: Exact terms use StringField; sorting needs doc values. Both are written at index time, then exposed by a reader refresh.

variants.title: Choose the field type
variants.context: TextField tokenizes text and indexes positions for phrase queries. StringField stores one exact term. Doc values provide per-document values for sorting and faceting. Stored fields return payloads but do not make a value searchable.
variants.prompt: Users search product descriptions with multi-word phrases. Which field type?
options: TextField, whose standard type indexes positions.
StringField.
A stored field only.
optionFeedback: TextField tokenizes and records positions, which phrase queries need.
StringField makes the entire description one term.
Stored fields return payloads; they do not make text searchable.
variants.hint: Which structure records where each word appears?
variants.explanation: Phrase queries need positions in the postings. Only an analyzed text field with positions can answer them.

variants.title: Choose the field type
variants.context: TextField tokenizes text and indexes positions for phrase queries. StringField stores one exact term. Doc values provide per-document values for sorting and faceting. Stored fields return payloads but do not make a value searchable.
variants.prompt: Results must be sorted by price and faceted by brand. Which structures are needed?
options: Doc values for price and brand.
Stored fields for price and brand.
Term vectors.
optionFeedback: Doc values give strongly typed per-document values for sorting and faceting.
Stored fields hydrate results; they are not built for column-style access.
Term vectors are optional per-document term statistics, not sort structures.
variants.explanation: Sorting and faceting read one value per document across many documents. That is what doc values provide.

variants.title: Choose the field type
variants.context: TextField tokenizes text and indexes positions for phrase queries. StringField stores one exact term. Doc values provide per-document values for sorting and faceting. Stored fields return payloads but do not make a value searchable.
variants.prompt: The team stored the full JSON payload in Lucene and expects it to be searchable. What is true?
options: Storage alone does not make a value searchable; a searchable structure must be indexed.
Stored fields are automatically tokenized.
Storing text creates doc values.
optionFeedback: A stored field returns bytes after another structure finds the document.
Stored fields are not analyzed.
Doc values are a separate structure chosen deliberately.
variants.hint: What does a stored field actually do?
variants.explanation: Store only what the result path must return. Large payloads can stay in the system of record and be hydrated by stable ID.

variants.title: Separate visibility from durability
variants.context: “Accepted by the writer”, “visible to a reader”, and “durable after a crash” are different states. A flush is not a commit; a near-real-time reader refresh gives visibility; commit plus fsync gives durability.
variants.prompt: Documents were added through IndexWriter, but searches do not return them. What is missing?
options: A reader refresh; the searcher still sees its older point-in-time view.
A larger heap.
A commit; searches require durable files.
optionFeedback: An IndexSearcher only sees the reader it was opened on; refresh to expose new changes.
Memory is not what gates visibility.
Commit gives durability, not visibility; a near-real-time reader can see uncommitted changes.
variants.hint: Which state controls what a searcher can see?
variants.explanation: Reader refresh and durable commit solve different problems. Refresh a reader or manager to publish a new view.

variants.title: Separate visibility from durability
variants.context: “Accepted by the writer”, “visible to a reader”, and “durable after a crash” are different states. A flush is not a commit; a near-real-time reader refresh gives visibility; commit plus fsync gives durability.
variants.prompt: The writer flushed, then the machine crashed before a commit. What happened to the flushed documents?
options: They may be lost; a flush is not an fsync commit.
They are safe because flush writes files.
They are safe because a reader saw them.
optionFeedback: Only a commit syncs referenced files so the commit point survives a crash.
Writing files without syncing does not guarantee survival.
Visibility to a reader says nothing about durability.
variants.hint: Which operation makes a commit point survive a crash?
variants.explanation: Flush moves buffered state into files; commit plus sync makes it durable. Neither should be inferred from the other.

variants.title: Separate visibility from durability
variants.context: “Accepted by the writer”, “visible to a reader”, and “durable after a crash” are different states. A flush is not a commit; a near-real-time reader refresh gives visibility; commit plus fsync gives durability.
variants.prompt: An application calls updateDocument with a term for the product ID. What does Lucene do?
options: Deletes documents matching the term and adds the complete replacement.
Edits the matching document in place.
Merges the new fields into the old document.
optionFeedback: Segments are immutable; an update is a delete plus an add.
Nothing is edited in place in an immutable segment.
There is no partial merge; the whole document is replaced.
variants.hint: Segments are immutable. What does that imply for an update?
variants.explanation: An update is implemented as delete-by-term followed by adding the full replacement document. Deleted documents consume space until merges reclaim them.

variants.title: Keep identity stable
variants.context: Index a stable domain ID as an exact term and use it for replacement or deletion. Internal Lucene document numbers are ephemeral. Carry a source version to reject stale writes.
variants.prompt: A service stores Lucene’s internal document number as the product’s ID. What goes wrong?
options: Document numbers change as documents are added, deleted, or merged.
Nothing; document numbers are permanent.
Searches become slower.
optionFeedback: Internal numbers are ephemeral and are not stable external IDs.
They can change after merges and deletes.
Performance is not the issue; identity is.
variants.hint: What happens to numbering after a merge?
variants.explanation: Index a stable domain ID as an exact term and use it for replacement and deletion.

variants.title: Keep identity stable
variants.context: Index a stable domain ID as an exact term and use it for replacement or deletion. Internal Lucene document numbers are ephemeral. Carry a source version to reject stale writes.
variants.prompt: Events arrive out of order and an older version overwrites a newer product document. What prevents this?
options: Carry a source version and reject stale writes before replacing the document.
Retry the update.
Use a larger merge factor.
optionFeedback: Version checks stop an old event from replacing newer state.
Retrying repeats the wrong order.
Merges do not order business events.
variants.hint: What tells you which write is newer?
variants.explanation: Out-of-order delivery needs a source version in the document and a check that rejects stale writes.

variants.title: Keep identity stable
variants.context: Index a stable domain ID as an exact term and use it for replacement or deletion. Internal Lucene document numbers are ephemeral. Carry a source version to reject stale writes.
variants.prompt: After deleting many documents, index size does not shrink. Why?
options: Deleted documents consume space until segment merges reclaim them.
Deletes failed silently.
Lucene never reclaims space.
optionFeedback: A delete marks documents; merges rewrite segments without them.
The deletes applied; reclamation is deferred.
Merges do reclaim space over time or when forced deliberately.
variants.hint: What does a delete do to an immutable segment?
variants.explanation: Deletes are markers on immutable segments. Space returns when merges rewrite those segments.
